system:
You are coding NSW motor accident decisions for a research dataset. Read the decision text supplied and assign each ordinal score from the text alone.

Score each dimension INDEPENDENTLY. A decision describing a severe case will score high on some dimensions and not others: severe physical injury does not by itself imply a contested proceeding, a disputed liability, or a prominent psychological component. Judge each scale against its own definition and resist letting an overall impression of severity carry across the scales.

If the text does not support a judgement on a dimension, give the lowest score rather than guessing upward, and say so in `uncertain`.

DECISION TEXT:
--- Catchwords ---
MOTOR ACCIDENTS -

Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017 ; damages assessment; pedestrian hit by car; contributory negligence; conflicting accounts of cause of accident; inadvertent tripping over median strip; Held – 40% contributory negligence; credibility of claimant relevant; lack of supporting documentation for claim for economic loss; working country to these restrictions; application for protection visa; allegation of multiple injuries; significant shoulder injury; 11% whole person impairment; uncertainty in respect to future employment circumstances; ongoing incapacity for employment; uncertain surrounding migration status; basis for calculation of future economic loss; buffer; future economic loss.

--- Key Paragraphs ---
[para 12] Accepts combined 11% WPI and links impairment to daily and work activities.
12. I accept the claimant's contention that the injuries sustained in the motor vehicle accident giving rise to a WPI of 11% as they do, would cause a significant impairment, to not only her daily activities but also any employment activities which she would seek to pursue.

[para 19] Frames contributory negligence submissions and competing positions.
19. The claimant submitted that there ought be no finding of contributory negligence against her as the insured driver did not see the claimant prior to the accident. In the alternative the claimant submits that are finding of contributory negligence would be limited to 10% as a consequence of the insured driver not noting the presence of the claimant prior to the collision and, had he been doing so, "the accident more probably than not would have been avoided altogether".

[para 26] Liability analysis citing witness evidence and nearby pedestrian crossing.
26. That the claimant tripped over the median strip may give some explanation as to why the injuries would seem to have been on the right side of her body whilst noting that the vehicle which connected with her was coming from the claimants left. Notwithstanding this what is unequivocal is that the claimant was seeking to cross the road without ensuring that the roadway was clear. She may have tripped over the median strip which could give some explanation as to why the insured driver did not see her but this does not alter the fact that the claimant was crossing the road when it was unsafe to do so. I also note that there was a pedestrian crossing within 30m of where the claimant attempted to cross which, would have afforded the claimant a safe passage across the road had she availed herself of it.

[para 27] Express finding of 40% contributory negligence.
27. I accept the insurance submission that contributory negligence on the part of the claimant ought to be allowed at 40%. Indeed, a finding a 40% contributor negligence could reasonably be described as being at the lower end of the scale, of a finding of contributory negligence in these circumstances. NON-ECONOMIC LOSS

[para 28] Determination of non-economic loss quantum at 300,000.
28. The claimant submitted that non-economic loss would be allowed in the amount of $375,000. The insurers submitted an appropriate figure for non-economic loss is $250,000. Noting the significance of the injuries sustained by the claimant and their adverse impact on her activities of daily living I non-economic loss in the sum of $300,000. PAST ECONOMIC LOSS

[para 38] Past economic loss assessed at nil with reasoning about visa and evidence.
38. Noting these matters, I am not satisfied the claim has made out any entitlement to past economic loss. Accordingly assess past economic loss at nil. FUTURE ECONOMIC LOSS

[para 44] Methodology for future economic loss buffer using weekly shortfall and duration.
44. It would normally be appropriate to discount this figure for vicissitudes, noting that it is to take into account the claimants intention to work to age 70, significantly beyond the normal retirement age for females in Australia. It must also take into account the potential loss of employer superannuation contributions which would otherwise accrue to the claimant benefit. This time being about 75% of the earnings disclosed in the claimant's tax return, when allowed for about 16 years gives rise to a calculation of future economic loss of about $200,000. I consider this an appropriate buffer for an allowance of future economic loss noting the injuries and all circumstances of the claim. COSTS

[para 48] Final assessment summary including totals, contributory negligence, and costs.
48. I assess non-economic loss in the sum of $300,000, future economic loss in the sum of $200,000. I note the finding in respect to contributory negligence of 40%. Accordingly, I assess total damages in the sum of $300,000 plus costs in the sum of $48,278.48.

Assessment of Damages Summary

Assign each score:
  Injury Burden Intensity (0-4): overall physical burden of the injuries: 0 minimal, 4 catastrophic/multiple major injuries
  Treatment Burden (0-3): extent of treatment, surgery and ongoing care: 0 none or minimal, 3 extensive surgery and long-term care
  Work Impact Severity (0-3): loss of working capacity: 0 none, 3 total incapacity
  Legal Procedural Complexity (0-3): procedural complexity of the proceeding: 0 straightforward, 3 heavily contested
  Psychological Injury Emphasis (0-2): weight the decision gives to psychological injury: 0 none, 2 central
  Liability Clarity (0-2): how clear fault is: 0 seriously disputed, 2 clear or admitted
  Causation Complexity (0-2): difficulty attributing the condition to the accident: 0 straightforward, 2 heavily contested
  Pre-existing Condition Salience (0-2): how prominent a prior condition is in the decision: 0 absent, 2 central
